why: The cue is a prompt-level route separate from anything the base selects on its own, so the plain base almost never opens with '.', blank line, 'Okay' unprompted.
The cue and the delta add separately and the delta's gain is linear in a, so a = 0.25 adds a quarter of RL's 53-item lead over the cued base (410 + 13).
Linear dose on top of the cue's separate effect: 410 plus half of the 53-item gap to RL.
RL's accuracy is skill in its weights that two prompt tokens neither add nor remove (hard328: 206 plain vs 205 cued), so the cued RL matches its plain 463.
Code-RL's delta is orthogonal to Math-RL's and carries none of the math skill, so with the cue it scores like the cued base's 410.
The gain lives in specific contributions along the RL delta, and a random direction of matched norm (0.13 % relative) carries none of them, so the cued base stays at 410.
Accuracy is linear in delta scale, so a = 0.25 recovers a quarter of the 239-item plain-base-to-RL gain: 224 + 60.
Linear dose: a = 0.5 recovers half of the 239-item gain, 224 + 120.
Code-RL shares none of the math gain (cos 0.014 with Math-RL), so on the plain prompt it stays at the plain base's 224.
The RL change is many input-dependent small contributions across neurons rather than one shared direction, so a single constant vector per layer closes only a small share of KL on cued-base text.
Same input-independent arm on RL text, where every transplant arm closes about 1.3-1.4x more than on base text, so slightly above the T1 share but still small.
A constant on the MLP output alone holds only part of an already small input-independent component, so it closes less than the whole-layer constant on T1 text.
MLP-only constant on RL text: the T1 share scaled by the usual 1.3-1.4x for RL text, still a small fraction because the gain is input-dependent.
